abstract: |
  Large language models (LLMs) can grade answers to German law exams at scale. But the same answer
  gets different scores from different models, and even from one model on a second run. Some
  examiners grade with a grading sheet (*Bewertungsbogen*) that splits the expected solution into
  small steps worth fixed points. We ask whether a sheet that a model writes from the case and its
  reference solution makes LLM grades steadier, and at what cost to agreement with human graders. A
  first iteration on 15 exams and 45 human-graded answers used sheets from 12 models. On average the
  sheets did not make the stronger grading models (judges) steadier and tended to lower agreement
  with the human graders. With a sheet, several judges gave high scores to empty answers or to
  answers that only copy the case. In the rebuilt pipeline, one model writes small steps with
  explicit requirements, including paths for defensible alternative solutions and auxiliary opinions
  (*Hilfsgutachten*). The judge must back every point with a quote, and a fixed program checks that
  each quote stands in the answer. On the scripts of one police-law exam, graded on its author's own
  sheet, we test whether sheets make grades steadier and closer to the examiner's, which models write
  and use sheets well, and whether the pipeline meets German examination law. First runs on 15 scripts
  suggest that a sheet does not make repeated runs steadier, but brings the grades much closer to the
  examiner's. \pending{results of the full benchmark and the recommended pipeline}

```{python}
MINUS = "−"


def _q(x, nd):
    """Round half up from the value's decimal form (10.85 -> 10.9), not
    from its binary float (which would give 10.8)."""
    return Decimal(repr(float(x))).quantize(Decimal(1).scaleb(-nd), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)


def num(x, nd=2):
    return f"{_q(x, nd):.{nd}f}".replace("-", MINUS)


def sgn(x, nd=2):
    return f"{_q(x, nd):+.{nd}f}".replace("-", MINUS)


def cor(x, nd=2):
    """Correlations and p-values without the leading zero (.77, -.13)."""
    s = f"{abs(_q(x, nd)):.{nd}f}"
    s = s[1:] if s.startswith("0") else s
    return (MINUS if x < 0 else "") + s


def pv(p):
    return cor(p, 3) if p < 0.01 else cor(p, 2)


def pct(x, nd=0):
    return f"{_q(100 * x, nd):.{nd}f}%"


def ci(c, nd=2):
    """A 95% interval of a difference, in brackets as everywhere in the paper."""
    return f"[{sgn(c[0], nd)}, {sgn(c[1], nd)}]"


def cic(c):
    """A 95% interval of a correlation."""
    return f"[{cor(c[0])}, {cor(c[1])}]"


def rng(a, b, nd=1, sep="–"):
    return f"{num(a, nd)}{sep}{num(b, nd)}"


def usd(x, nd=0):
    return f"USD {x:,.{nd}f}"

def tex_escape(s):
    for a, b in (("\\", "\\textbackslash{}"), ("&", "\\&"), ("%", "\\%"), ("$", "\\$"),
                 ("#", "\\#"), ("_", "\\_"), ("{", "\\{"), ("}", "\\}")):
        s = s.replace(a, b)
    return s


def crit_tex(s):
    return tex_escape(s).replace(">=", "$\\geq$").replace("<=", "$\\leq$").replace("<", "$<$")


def write_table(name, caption, label, header, rows, colspec=None, size=r"\small", wide=False, note=None):
    """A captioned booktabs table in assets/<name>.tex, included with \\input
    (raw blocks with \\caption get mangled by Quarto's crossref pass)."""
    colspec = colspec or ("l" + "r" * (len(header) - 1))
    esc = lambda t: re.sub(r"(?<!\\)%", r"\\%", str(t))  # a bare % would start a LaTeX comment
    caption = esc(caption)
    rows = [r if r == "MIDRULE" else (esc(r) if isinstance(r, str) else [esc(c) for c in r]) for r in rows]
    lines = [r"\begin{table}[t]", rf"\caption{{{caption}}}", rf"\label{{{label}}}", r"\centering", size]
    if wide:
        lines.append(rf"\begin{{tabular*}}{{\textwidth}}{{@{{\extracolsep{{\fill}}}}{colspec}@{{}}}}")
    else:
        lines.append(rf"\begin{{tabular}}{{@{{}}{colspec}@{{}}}}")
    lines += [r"\toprule", " & ".join(header) + r" \\", r"\midrule"]
    for r in rows:
        if r == "MIDRULE":
            lines.append(r"\midrule")
        elif isinstance(r, str):
            lines.append(r + r" \\")
        else:
            lines.append(" & ".join(str(c) for c in r) + r" \\")
    lines += [r"\bottomrule", r"\end{tabular*}" if wide else r"\end{tabular}"]
    if note:
        lines += [r"\par\smallskip", rf"\parbox{{\textwidth}}{{\footnotesize {note}}}"]
    lines.append(r"\end{table}")
    (ASSETS / f"{name}.tex").write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print("```{=latex}\n\\input{assets/" + name + ".tex}\n```\n")
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

German law students learn and are examined through case solutions (*Falllösungen*). A candidate
receives a fact pattern (*Sachverhalt*) and writes a legal opinion in a prescribed appraisal style
(*Gutachtenstil*). The state examinations grade such opinions on a statutory scale from 0 to
`{python} V["R18"]` grade points [@jurprnotskv1981]. Different examiners often give the same answer
different grades [@hufeld2024]. Some correctors therefore first note what each part of the expected
solution is worth [@frenzel2011korrektur, p. 330]. A few examiners make this binding in a grading
sheet (*Bewertungsbogen*) [@heidebach2015pruefen; @strecker2026ki]. It splits the expected solution
into small steps, each worth some assessment units (*Bewertungseinheiten*, BE), and a key maps the BE
total to a grade. Appendix \ref{sec-app-glossary} lists the German terms and the technical terms we use.

Large language models (LLMs) can grade such texts at scale. An LLM used as a grader is called a
*judge*. On German case solutions, a judge that applies the same `{python} V["n_dims"]` general
criteria to every exam stays within the range of human disagreement, but its scores vary between
judges and between repeated runs [@nagl2026bengerdata]. For candidates this is a matter of equal
opportunity (*Chancengleichheit*): comparable candidates must be graded by comparable standards
[@bverfge84_34, p. 52]. We test the examiners' remedy. One model, the *generator*, writes an
exam-specific grading sheet from the case and its reference solution (*Musterlösung*), and the judge
grades against it. The sheet also gives the examiner a document to read and correct.

A first iteration tested this remedy on `{python} V["n_exams"]` exams with `{python} V["n_answers"]`
answers and blind human grades. On average the sheets did not make the stronger judges steadier, and
they tended to lower agreement with the human graders. With a sheet, several judges gave high scores
to empty answers or to answers that only copy the case (@sec-first). We then rebuilt the pipeline
from case to grade. We test it on the written answers (*scripts*) to a police-law exam set by one of
us and graded on the author's own sheet and key, and we ask what German examination law requires of such
grading.

- **RQ1 Variance.** Does a generated sheet make LLM grades steadier than grading without one, counting
  the scatter between runs, judges and the sheets one generator may write? Does it beat averaging
  several runs at equal cost?
- **RQ2 Validity.** How close are sheet-based grades to the examiner's and to a second human grader,
  and how many students would they wrongly pass or fail?
- **RQ3 Generators and judges.** Which models write sheets that yield grades close to the examiner's
  at low cost, and which judges use them well?
- **RQ4 Law.** Does sheet-based grading meet what German examination law asks of grading, on
  defensible (*vertretbar*) alternative solutions, follow-on errors (*Folgefehler*), reasons for each
  point and equal opportunity, and which uses does the evidence support?

Our contributions are:

1. A pipeline that turns doctrine into checkable structure (@sec-pipeline): steps with explicit
   requirements, separate paths for defensible alternative solutions, owed auxiliary opinions
   (*Hilfsgutachten*), and points only for quotes that a fixed program finds in the answer.
2. A study of all scripts of one exam that splits the scatter of grades into its sources (runs,
   judges, sheets) and compares sheets with averaging runs at equal cost (RQ1).
3. Agreement with the examiner, a second human grader and the examiner's own second grading,
   counting the students an LLM would wrongly pass or fail (RQ2), and a small benchmark of generators
   and judges (RQ3).
4. A legal analysis, co-written with the exam's author, that maps each requirement of examination law
   to a design feature and a test (@sec-practice, RQ4).

# Grading practice in German law exams {#sec-practice}

\draftnote{to be co-written with the exam author; every pending item below needs the author's input or experiments E2, E4 and E5}

*The setting.* The statutory scale has `{python} V["bands"]` grades (*Notenstufen*) from 0 to
`{python} V["R18"]` grade points. `{python} V["pass_np"]` points (*ausreichend*, "sufficient") is the
lowest grade that still meets average requirements despite its flaws [@jurprnotskv1981, § 1]. In
practice a single exam is passed from this grade; the rules on passing are state (*Land*) law.
Examiners set their own standards for an exam and must apply them to every script alike
[@bverwg2018_6B71_17]. University exams usually have one grader [@strecker2026ki, p. 29]. Some
correctors first build a private point scheme [@frenzel2011korrektur, p. 330], and a few examiners
make it binding in a sheet [@heidebach2015pruefen]. Such sheets are rare [@strecker2026ki, p. 3]. Two
principles bind any sheet. A defensible solution (*vertretbare Lösung*), consistently argued with
weighty reasons, must not be marked as wrong. For exams that control access to a profession this
follows from Art. 12(1) GG [@bverfge84_34, p. 55]. And a follow-on error (*Folgefehler*) should cost
points only once. A later step that correctly builds on the candidate's own earlier decision still
earns credit. \pending{exam author: source for the follow-on-error principle}

*Three paradigms.* We compare three ways of grading with our sheet (Table \ref{tab:paradigms}). The
exam author's sheet (D2) is a list of steps with absolute BE, grouped into sections. Gregor Roth's
sheet for a civil-law exam (Z2) is a tree. Each item carries a percentage of the item above it. Each
of the `{python} Z2["weighted_leaves"]` smallest items gets a grade from
`{python} num(Z2["leaf_grade_range"][0], 0)` to `{python} num(Z2["leaf_grade_range"][1], 0)`, and the
final grade is their average, weighted by these percentages. This method needs no key
[@strecker2026ki, p. 12]. A third practice is
common as well: about `{python} pct(PF["fixed_share"])` of the BE go to steps, and the grader
distributes the remaining `{python} pct(PF["free_share"])` freely, for instance for structure or the
overall impression. We do not adopt it: the free share is tied to nothing in the answer that a
second grader or a judge could check, so it invites variance and cannot be reproduced. Our sheet
follows the first paradigm. Every BE, in half points, belongs to a step. Each step lists the
requirements that earn it, and code does all arithmetic (@sec-pipeline).

*Q1: How should the BE be distributed?* The author's sheet spreads `{python} D2["sheet"]["total_be"]`
BE over `{python} D2["sheet"]["n_steps"]` steps with at most `{python} num(D2["sheet"]["max_step_be"], 0)`
BE per step. Some step weights changed between years (@sec-d2) \pending{exam author: why}. We took
the step-size guidance of
our generator (`{python} num(GEN["step_be_guidance"][0], 1)` to `{python} num(GEN["step_be_guidance"][1], 0)`
BE per step, at most `{python} num(GEN["max_step_be"], 0)` BE) from the two expert sheets, so step
size is an input of our design, not a finding. E3 compares the BE distributions of generated sheets
with the author's sheet and E5 with Roth's. \pending{BE distribution of the expert sheet and of generated sheets (E3)}

*Q2: What earns credit, including method?* In the author's sheet every step credits an issue
spotted or an argument made. No step credits a bare result; some step titles state a sub-result
instead. Our generator follows the same rule. A result earns credit only with the reasoning that
carries it. Where several results are defensible, the requirements credit the argument
[@bverfge84_34, p. 55]. The exam author credits method (structure, appraisal style, precise
language) inside each section, not as a separate block [@strecker2026ki, p. 14]. \pending{exam
author: confirm for D2} The first iteration kept style outside the points.


*Q3: Where is the pass mark?* The author's key passes a script at
`{python} pct(D2["sheet"]["pass_share"])` of the BE. The platform's default key, which the
first iteration used when grading without a sheet, passes at `{python} num(KEY["pass_percent"], 0)`%.
Where the pass mark lies is part of the examiner's own evaluation. It cannot be fixed rigidly
without regard to average results [@bverfge84_34, p. 51], and once set it applies to every script
alike [@bverwg2018_6B71_17]. The mark decides which students a judge passes or fails differently
from the examiner. E2 sweeps it from
`{python} pct(EXP["E2"]["pass_mark_sweep"][0])` to `{python} pct(EXP["E2"]["pass_mark_sweep"][1])`
on stored outputs. \pending{E2}

*Q4: Is the key linear or curved?* The author's key is piecewise linear with a kink at the pass
mark: below it a grade point spans `{python} D2["sheet"]["key_be_per_grade_below_pass"]` BE, from the
pass mark upwards `{python} D2["sheet"]["key_be_per_grade_from_pass"]` BE, up to grade 18 at
`{python} D2["sheet"]["key_top_grade_be"]` BE. The same shape, with passing costing more BE per
grade than the top grades, is proposed in [@strecker2026ki, p. 15]. \pending{exam author: confirm the
reasons for D2} The platform's
default key has the same shape: below the pass mark a grade point spans
`{python} num(KEY["mean_band_width_below_pass"], 1)` percentage points of the total on average, from
the pass mark upwards `{python} num(KEY["mean_band_width_from_pass"], 1)`. Roth's paradigm needs no
key: it averages statutory grades and passes from grade `{python} Z2["workbook"]["pass_from_grade"]`.

*Q5: How are cardinal errors treated?* A cardinal error (*Kardinalfehler*) is one that by itself can
make a script fail. Examiners disagree on what counts, and the literature asks each sheet to define
it in advance, with minus points or a grade cap [@strecker2026ki, pp. 15 f.]. \pending{exam author:
examples and expected loss for D2} Our sheet has no such cap yet. The follow-on-error rule and the
standard of each requirement decide how far an early error carries (@sec-judge). E4 tests `{python} EXP["E4"]["kardinalfehler_probes"]` fake answers with the losses
the author expects.

# Related work {#sec-related}

*Grading with LLMs.* A judge reads an answer and returns a score. Such judges agree with human
graders on average [@zheng2023mtbench; @liu2023geval] but are less dependable on a single answer.
The same answer can get a different score when graded again [@haldar2025rating; @schroeder2024trust].
Scores change when answers are shown in another order [@wang2024fair; @shi2024judging], and judges
favour texts written by their own model [@panickssery2024self]. A grader can also be steady and
still wrong [@jade2026chatgpt; @xue2026consistency]. Each use must therefore be checked against
human graders [@gu2024survey; @bavaresco2025llms; @calderon2025alternative]. Testing research splits
score differences into parts due to the student, the grader and the occasion (generalizability
theory) [@brennan2001generalizability]. This has been applied to LLM graders [@song2026exploring;
@wang2025evaluating], and the wording of the grading prompt has been treated as one such part
[@messing2026hidden]. Most fixes change the grader, for example by pooling several models
[@verga2024replacing]. We change the sheet the grader uses, and we count the sheet a model happens to
write as a source of differences of its own.

*Grading sheets written by models.* A rubric is a scoring guide that states what earns credit. A
checklist breaks it into yes-or-no items. Such items can make LLM grading more consistent
[@ye2024flask; @kim2024prometheus; @lee2025checkeval; @cook2024ticking; @chen2026holistic], and rubrics
written for one question work better than general ones [@jonsson2007use; @pathak2025rubric;
@tang2026designing]. Human graders also agree more when they score an answer part by part than when
they form one overall impression, at a cost in time [@klein1998analytic]; for an LLM the time becomes
computing cost. Models can write such rubrics. They derive weighted criteria from a reference answer
[@gunjal2025rubrics; @fan2024sedareval; @li2026rubrichub] and point schemes for exam questions and
proofs [@golchin2025grading; @xie2025grade; @mahdavi2025refgrader; @ma2026proofbench]. Generated
rubrics still fall short of expert ones [@zhou2026rubricbench; @wu2026unveiling], and a regenerated
marking scheme graded less accurately than the one the human graders had used [@ma2026proofbench].
Models that add up points themselves make mistakes [@kortemeyer2024grading; @pires2025automatic], so
our generator states only relative weights and code allocates the points. Our sheet also encodes two
rules of examination law: defensible alternative solutions, and follow-on errors that cost points
only once.

*Evidence and gaming.* Attribution research asks whether a text is backed by the sources it cites
[@rashkin2023measuring; @gao2023alce]. Some systems require exact quotes and check them in code
[@menick2022gophercite; @khan2024debating; @hong2026rulers]. Automated scoring has long been open to
gaming by padding, nonsense or keyword lists [@powers2002stumping; @ding2020dont], and LLM graders can
be steered by instructions hidden in an answer [@chiang2024large; @li2026important]. Our judge must
quote the answer for every credit. Code removes a credit whose quote is missing or turned into its
opposite, and fake answers test every judge before use.

*Grading law exams.* Research first asked whether LLMs pass law exams [@choi2023chatgpt;
@katz2024gpt4; @martinez2025reevaluating] and now asks whether they can grade them. The graders
receive model answers, marked passages, or rubrics written by experts or exam offices
[@fan2026lexam; @chlapanis2025greekbarbench; @shi2026plawbench; @pires2025automatic;
@pires2026magisbench; @cope2026grading; @akarajaradwong2026thai]. Others split answers into single
legal points [@enguehard2025lemaj] or derive issue trees from court judgments [@lee2026legit].
German examiners disagree widely [@hufeld2024]. An examiner's own point scheme cut the spread between
human correctors by almost half [@strecker2026ki], and LLM grades have been validated against the
same examiner's grades on the examiner's own scheme [@zubaer2026gradelegal]. To our knowledge, no
study on law exams has a model write the point scheme from the reference solution, with scoreable
paths for defensible alternatives and a follow-on-error standard per requirement, and tests the
result against the examiner's own sheet and grades.

# The pipeline {#sec-pipeline}

sheet and says how much each part weighs. The judge grades an answer against the sheet and quotes
the answer for every credit. Plain code, a fixed program and not a model, does everything that can
be computed or checked. Models that add up points themselves make mistakes [@kortemeyer2024grading;
@pires2025automatic], so no model ever states points.

## Generation: the checklist sheet {#sec-generation}

The generator receives the case text, the reference solution and fixed instructions, the same for
every model (Appendix \ref{sec-app-spec}). It returns a *checklist sheet* with these parts:

- *Sections and steps.* Each step names one expected legal performance and carries a relative
  weight. The exam's focal problems (*Klausurschwerpunkte*) are marked groups of steps. Each step
  belongs to a work result (*Arbeitsergebnis*), such as an opinion or a draft judgment.
- *Requirements.* Each step lists `{python} GEN["bullets_per_step"][0]` to
  `{python} GEN["bullets_per_step"][1]` requirements, each with a share of the step and a standard
  (*Maßstab*). A requirement is either correct (*richtig*), judged against the correct law, or
  consistent (*folgerichtig*), judged against the candidate's own earlier decision. The latter
  carries the follow-on-error rule. Each requirement names something the answer must write, which a
  quote can show. None may be met by leaving something out, none may be conditional, and none may
  ask only for a norm, a term or a result.
- *Forks and alternative paths.* A dispute that changes only a result or its reasons stays inside one
  step, and its requirement credits the argument, whatever the result. A structural fork
  (*Weichenstellung*) exists only where another defensible decision removes or adds steps. Each
  alternative path (*Lösungsweg*) has its own steps, its defensibility requirements
  (*Vertretbarkeitsanforderungen*), and the same BE as the steps it replaces.
- *Auxiliary opinions* (*Hilfsgutachten*). A step can be marked as owed even when the candidate's own
  decision cuts it off, for instance when a contractual claim already fails at formation.

The model states weights, never points.

## Points, checks and grades by code {#sec-allocation}

Code turns the weights into `{python} GEN["total_be"]` BE in half points. It uses the
largest-remainder method known from seat allocation (Hamilton, in Germany Hare-Niemeyer)
[@balinski2001fair]. Each step first gets the whole half points its weight earns, and the leftover
half points go to the steps with the largest remainders. Every step gets at least
`{python} num(GEN["min_step_be"], 1)` BE, and a heavier step never gets fewer points than a lighter
one. A requirement is worth its share of the step, and an alternative path is worth the steps it
replaces. The first iteration's routine broke these rules in `{python} AP["affected_rubrics"]` of
`{python} AP["n_rubrics"]` sheets (Appendix \ref{sec-app-apportionment}).

A program, the *validator*, then checks the sheet against fixed rules (Appendix
\ref{sec-app-validator}). Hard rules cover the structure, every cross-reference, the rules for
requirements and forks, and the cap of `{python} num(GEN["max_step_be"], 0)` BE per step. If one
fails, the generator gets its sheet back with the error messages and tries again, up to
`{python} GEN["max_attempts"]` times. Soft rules only log a warning. The rules compare words, so two
steps that say the same thing in other words both pass. Every sheet records the hashes of the
validator and of the instructions.

At the end, code adds up the credited points, rounds the total once to half points and maps it to a
grade with the exam's key. Several runs can be averaged.

## Judging {#sec-judge}

Code formats the sheet as text for the judge. The judge receives the case, the reference solution,
the sheet and the answer, each clearly marked, and answers in a fixed format. We test two scoring
units. In the *requirement* unit the judge marks each requirement as met, partly met or not met,
which earns `{python} num(JDG["status_credit"]["2"], 0)`, `{python} num(JDG["status_credit"]["1"], 1)`
or `{python} num(JDG["status_credit"]["0"], 0)` times its BE. In the *step* unit it awards each step
up to its BE in half points, as on a classic sheet. Every credit needs a word-for-word quote from the
answer. The judge follows fixed rules:

- *Placement.* Work counts for the step whose requirement it meets, even if it stands elsewhere in
  the same question and work result. It counts once. Work on another question counts only if the
  answer refers to it.
- *Follow-on errors.* Requirements with the consistent standard are judged on the answer's own
  earlier decisions. Other requirements are judged on the correct law, but an error that has already
  cost points is not charged again.
- *Auxiliary opinions.* Work on questions that the answer's own decision cut off earns credit like
  work in the main opinion. It never replaces the main result.
- *Alternatives.* The judge scores the steps of every path and names, with a quote, the path the
  answer follows. A path counts only if the answer gives the reasons its defensibility requirements
  demand. Code counts the named path (design A2); E4 compares two other designs (Appendix
  \ref{sec-app-alternatives}).
- *Unforeseen paths.* If the answer takes a defensible path that the sheet does not foresee, the judge
  credits the corresponding step at equal depth of reasoning and flags the script for human review.
- *General rules.* Contradictory results without a decision fail the requirement on the result.
  Unnecessary alternative analyses earn nothing. Length, many citations and strings of keywords are
  not performance, and a short, correct application meets a requirement fully.

The judge is told to ignore instructions inside its inputs, and a probe tests this. It also writes
short feedback for the candidate, which never changes points.

## The quote check and its limits {#sec-verifier}

Code checks that every quote really stands in the answer (Appendix \ref{sec-app-verifier}). It
tolerates small differences in layout, inflection and typing. Words that change the meaning must
match exactly: negations, result words such as *rechtmäßig* and *rechtswidrig* (lawful, unlawful),
qualifiers and numbers. A quote also fails if a negation or a condition stands right next to it. A
credit whose quote fails is set to zero.

The check has limits. It tests that a quote exists, not that it proves the requirement. A real
sentence can be quoted for the wrong requirement. Correct work that the judge paraphrases earns
nothing, and a sentence copied from the case text passes. The strict rules at the edges also reject
some correct quotes. The first iteration had no quote check.
\pending{regression replays at the freeze: quotes re-checked on D1, D2 and the stored D2b grades, and how many flip}

The experiments vary the generator, the judge, the scoring unit, the design for alternative paths
and the number of averaged runs. The baselines are grading without a sheet, on the prior study's
`{python} V["n_dims"]` general criteria, and grading on the exam author's own sheet. Options that the
code supports but that we do not test here are listed in Appendix \ref{sec-app-options}.

## D1: the first-iteration corpus {#sec-d1}

D1 holds the `{python} V["n_exams"]` exams of the BenGER corpus [@nagl2026bengerdata]. Three blind
graders and the exam's creator, who was not blind, graded every answer out of 100 points on the
prior study's `{python} V["n_dims"]` general criteria, the same criteria its LLM judge used. The blind
graders often disagree: their highest and lowest grade for an answer lie `{python} V["spread"]` points
apart on average. @sec-first compares with the mean of all `{python} V["pool"]` grades on the
`{python} V["n_ann"]` answers written by people, as the prior study did. The new experiments use the
blind grades as the main reference and the creator's grade as a second one. The prior study's judge
was `{python} V["prior_mae"]` points (`{python} V["prior_mae_np"]` grade points) from the mean human
grade on average and ranked the answers much as the humans did ($r$ = `{python} V["prior_r"]`). D1 is
our only data across many exams, but its reference is noisy.

## D2: the expert exam {#sec-d2}

D2 is one police-law exam from LMU, set each year from 2024 to 2026. Its author is a co-author of this
paper. The author's sheet has `{python} D2["sheet"]["n_steps"]` steps worth
`{python} D2["sheet"]["total_be"]` BE in half points, and the author's key passes a script at
`{python} pct(D2["sheet"]["pass_share"])`. Some step weights changed between years, so the sheet
exists in `{python} D2["sheet"]["n_states"]` versions with the same steps. The judge always sees the
current one.

- *D2a* holds `{python} D2["d2a"]["n_scripts"]` typed scripts, `{python} D2["d2a"]["by_year"]["2024"]`
  from 2024 and `{python} D2["d2a"]["by_year"]["2025"]` from 2025, graded
  step by step on the sheet version then in use. We call these *reference grades*, because for
  `{python} D2["d2a"]["grader_pending"]` scripts the grader is still being confirmed.
- *D2b* holds `{python} D2["d2b"]["n_students"]` student scripts from 2026, written on our platform as
  a practice exam. We drop `{python} D2["d2b"]["n_excluded"]` uploads from the author's own account (a
  test upload and a copy of a D2a script). The platform graded the scripts on submission with GPT-5.4
  Mini, and the students saw these grades. The author now grades them blind, without seeing any
  model grade. \pending{blind expert grades for D2b}

D2 thus has `{python} D2["distinct_scripts"]` distinct scripts, or
`{python} D2["n_counting_dependent_pair_once"]` if one pair that shares text counts once. We lack the
2024 case text, so the `{python} D2["d2a"]["later_case_text"]` scripts of 2024 are judged against a
later one. \pending{the 2024 case text from the exam author}

All D2 texts were pseudonymized and checked for personal data before any research call to a model
provider (Appendix \ref{sec-app-datastatement}). No generator and no judge without a sheet sees the
author's sheet. A canary check confirms that the fixed instructions and examples in every prompt
contain no terms from the author's sheet or exam.

*Z2* is Gregor Roth's sheet and grading workbook for a civil-law exam, so far without case, reference
solution or scripts. E5 generates sheets for this exam and compares them with Roth's sheet.
\pending{case and reference solution from Roth}

## Experiments {#sec-experiments}

We built the pipeline on D1 and D2a. D2b is held out. It holds new scripts of the same exam, not a
new exam. The author grades them from exported scripts before seeing any generated sheet or model
grade, and one registered test runs on them once. \pending{the registered hypothesis and its success
criterion} Stability needs no human grade, so E1 uses all `{python} D2["distinct_scripts"]` D2 scripts.
Table \ref{tab:experiments} lists the experiments. On the author's sheet, which has no requirements,
the judge scores per step; generated sheets are scored both ways, so that the sheet and the scoring
unit can be told apart. The whole program costs `{python} usd(COST["experiments_sum_usd"][0])` to
`{python} COST["experiments_sum_usd"][1]` at list prices (Appendix \ref{sec-app-costs}).

```{python}
#| output: asis
erows = [[e["id"], e["name"], ", ".join(e["rq"]), tex_escape(e["scope"])] for e in DZ["experiments"]]
write_table(
    "tbl_experiments", "Experiments of the extended study. \\pending{actual costs per experiment}",
    "tab:experiments", ["", "Experiment", "RQ", "What we do"], erows,
    colspec="lp{0.16\\textwidth}p{0.1\\textwidth}p{0.6\\textwidth}", size=r"\footnotesize")
```

*Measures.* Accuracy is the average distance of a total from the human grade (mean absolute error,
MAE), its sign (bias: too generous or too strict), the error in grade points on the 0 to
`{python} V["R18"]` scale, and the students a model passes or fails differently from the human grade. For stability we split the spread of totals into
real differences between scripts and noise from the judge, from the sheet a generator happens to
write and from repeated runs [@brennan2001generalizability]. Dependability, from 0 to 1, is the share
of the spread that reflects real differences between scripts when a single run decides. We also count
how often a second run lands on the other side of the pass mark [@livingston1995estimating] and
compare sheets with averaging runs at equal cost. Each human reference was graded with one method,
D1 on the `{python} V["n_dims"]` general criteria and D2 on the author's sheet, so each favours the
grading basis it shares.

*Fake answers (probes).* Before any benchmark run, every judge and sheet must clear a set of fake
answers in each of `{python} DZ["probes"]["passes"]` runs (Appendix \ref{sec-app-probes}). Empty,
copied, off-topic or manipulative answers must score about zero, and the reference solution must
score high. Cutting one section of the reference solution must cost about its BE, and moving correct
reasoning under another heading almost nothing.

*Uncertainty.* Apart from the registered test, we estimate and do not test. Every range is a 95%
interval from redrawing exams (D1) or scripts (D2) many times (bootstrap). With
`{python} D2["d2a"]["n_scripts"]` graded scripts only large differences are visible (Appendix
\ref{sec-app-precision}). Each judge runs at one fixed temperature in all comparisons. Scripts that the
judge flags for review keep their totals in our analyses.

*Development runs.* Small runs on D1 and D2 and `{python} DZ["statistics"]["review_rounds"]`
automated review rounds (@sec-ai) shaped the pipeline. They used an earlier version. @sec-prelim
reports the D2 runs as first signals; they do not enter the registered test. All runs of the
extended study so far cost `{python} usd((GEN2 or {}).get("study_spend_usd", COST["development_spend_usd"]), 2)`.

# Results {#sec-results}

Totals are points out of 100. A grade point is one step on the 0 to `{python} V["R18"]` scale. On the
expert exam, `{python} D2["sheet"]["key_be_per_grade_from_pass"]` points make one grade point from the
pass mark (`{python} num(D2["sheet"]["pass_share"] * D2["sheet"]["total_be"], 0)` points) up and
`{python} D2["sheet"]["key_be_per_grade_below_pass"]` below it. $r$ says whether two graders rank the
scripts in the same order (1 = the same order); it ignores a constant shift. Brackets give 95%
intervals. If the interval of a difference includes zero, we cannot tell whether the difference is
real.

The first iteration tested an earlier, richer sheet on D1. Each step carried a weight class,

judges graded the `{python} V["n_answers"]` answers `{python} passes` times with that sheet
(`{python} len(JU["extra_single_pass"])` more once), and
`{python} len(CO["per_judge"])` of them also without a sheet, on the prior study's
`{python} V["n_dims"]` general criteria [@nagl2026bengerdata]. Totals are sums of the step scores
(Appendix \ref{sec-app-corrections}).

*Writing sheets worked.* `{python} V["n_valid"]` of `{python} V["n_cells"]` generator–exam pairs
yielded a valid sheet, and `{python} V["n_full"]` of the `{python} V["n_gens"]` generators covered
every exam. The sheets differed widely: the mean number of steps per generator ranged from
`{python} num(G["step_count_mean_range"][0], 0)` to `{python} num(G["step_count_mean_range"][1], 0)`
(Table \ref{tab:compliance}).

```{python}
    f"Run-to-run spread: standard deviation of a judge's total over {passes} runs on the same answer "
    f"({FI['reliability']['repeat_n']} answers). The other columns compare the first run with the mean of the "
    f"four human grades (three blind graders and the exam's creator) on the {FI['reliability']['agreement_n']} "
    "answers written by people. "
    + (f"{DAG}Stored total. " if any(REL[k]["basis"] in ("step_sum", "stored_pending") for k in REL) else "")
    + "Sheets written from an example: Appendix \\ref{sec-app-first}.",
    "tab:reliability", ["Judge, grading basis", "Run-to-run spread", "Same order ($r$)", "Average error",
                        "Too generous (+) / strict ($-$)"], rows,
    colspec="lp{0.14\\textwidth}p{0.12\\textwidth}p{0.11\\textwidth}p{0.17\\textwidth}", size=r"\footnotesize")
six = statistics.fmean(f["delta"] for f in CO["per_judge"])
mini_ci_has_zero = mini_f["ci95"][0] < 0 < mini_f["ci95"][1]
```

*The sheets did not make grading steadier* (Table \ref{tab:reliability}). Graded again, Luna's total
for the same answer moved by `{python} num(REL["holistic_luna"]["repeat_sd"], 1)` points without a
sheet and `{python} num(REL["tailored_luna"]["repeat_sd"], 1)` with one (standard deviation over runs).
Across the `{python} pooled["n_judges"]` judges other than GPT-5.4 Mini, the sheet changed this spread
by `{python} sgn(pooled["point"])` points on average `{python} ci(pooled["ci95"])`, and Claude Sonnet
4.6 was steadier without a sheet (Table \ref{tab:contrasts}). With GPT-5.4 Mini included, the average
would be `{python} sgn(six)`. GPT-5.4 Mini's own spread grew from
`{python} num(REL["holistic_mini"]["repeat_sd"], 1)` to `{python} num(REL["tailored_mini"]["repeat_sd"], 1)`
points`{python} ", although its interval includes no change" if mini_ci_has_zero else ""`. The
judges disagreed with one another far more than with themselves: the standard deviation of the
`{python} FI["reliability"]["panel_size"]` judges' totals for the same answer was `{python} num(prs[0], 0)` to `{python} num(prs[1], 0)` points.

*Nor did the sheets bring the grades closer to the humans.* With the sheet, Luna ranked the answers
about as before ($r$ = `{python} cor(AG["luna"]["zs_step_sum"]["r"])` against
`{python} cor(AG["luna"]["hol"]["r"])`) but turned from `{python} num(AG["luna"]["hol"]["bias"], 0)`
points too generous to `{python} num(abs(REL["tailored_luna"]["bias"]), 0)` points too strict. GPT-5.4
Mini's average error rose from `{python} num(AG["mini"]["hol"]["mae"], 0)` to
`{python} num(AG["mini"]["zs_step_sum"]["mae"], 0)` points.

*The sheets invited credit for nothing.* With a sheet, Luna gave a near-empty answer about
`{python} num(PR["luna_empty_mean_failing"]["tailored"], 0)` of 100 points in
`{python} fc["tailored"][LUNA]["empty"]` of `{python} npas["tailored"][LUNA]["empty"]` runs, and
`{python} "never did so without one" if fc["holistic"][LUNA]["empty"] == 0 else "rarely without one"`.
GPT-5.4 Mini gave empty answers a median of `{python} num(sev["tailored"][MINI]["empty"]["median"], 0)`
points. Only `{python} " and ".join(NAME[j] for j in PR["clean_battery"])` kept every fake answer near
zero on every run (Table \ref{tab:probes}).

An automated review of the sheets by GPT-5.4 Mini did not predict which sheets graded well, and it
favoured sheets that graded harshly (Table \ref{tab:generators}). The generated weights carried
little signal, and big steps were not noisier per point than small ones (Appendices
\ref{sec-app-weights} and \ref{sec-app-steps}). Appendix \ref{sec-app-first} gives the details.

We attribute these failures mainly to the first-iteration pipeline. It checked no quotes, listed the
steps out of outline order, and gave the steps of alternative paths no fields of their own (Appendix
\ref{sec-app-corrections}). The rebuilt pipeline (@sec-pipeline) addresses each defect, and E0 and E3
test again whether weaker judges can use a sheet safely.

```{python}
def _v(arm, judge):
    return ((VAL2 or {}).get("per_arm", {}).get(arm, {}) or {}).get(judge)


def _c(a, b):
    for c in (VAL2 or {}).get("contrasts", []):
        if (c["a"]["judge"], c["a"]["arm"]) == a and (c["b"]["judge"], c["b"]["arm"]) == b:
            return c
    return None


def _d(x, nd=1):
    """A paired difference with its bootstrap interval."""
    return f"{sgn(x['mean_diff'], nd)} [{sgn(x['ci95'][0], nd)}, {sgn(x['ci95'][1], nd)}]"


def RP(w):
    """A right-aligned paragraph column of width w (share of the text width)."""
    return r">{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{%.2f\textwidth}" % w


def _n1(v):
    """One decimal, without a trailing .0 (counts averaged over runs)."""
    t = num(v, 1)
    return t[:-2] if t.endswith(".0") else t


def _wrong(x):
    return f"{_n1(x['wrong_pass'])} / {_n1(x['wrong_fail'])}"


_mdes = [c["abs_error"]["mde"] for c in (VAL2 or {}).get("contrasts", []) if c["abs_error"].get("mde")]
_ref = next(iter(next(iter((VAL2 or {}).get("per_arm", {}).values()), {}).values()), None)
LV = ((VAR2 or {}).get("per_judge", {}) or {}).get(LU, {})
```

These runs are a first look at the expert exam, not the benchmark. They used the pipeline as it stood
(an earlier output specification), sheets from two generators and up to three judges. With
`{python} D2["d2a"]["n_scripts"]` graded scripts, only differences in average error of about
`{python} num(min(_mdes), 1) if _mdes else "?"` to `{python} num(max(_mdes), 1) if _mdes else "?"`
points can be told apart from chance (80% power; Appendix \ref{sec-app-precision}), so these are first
signals, not a ranking. The yardstick is the reference grades of the D2a scripts. They were given on
the examiner's own sheet, which favours that sheet over generated ones, and for
`{python} D2["d2a"]["grader_pending"]` scripts the grader is still being confirmed. The reference
fails `{python} _ref["reference_n_fail"] if _ref else "?"` of the `{python} D2["d2a"]["n_scripts"]` scripts.

## The redesigned experiments (E1 to E5)

\pending{E1 to E5}. E1 splits the spread of totals on all D2 scripts into differences between
scripts and noise from runs, judges and the sheet a generator happens to write, gives the
dependability of each grading basis and the share of pass/fail flips, and compares sheets with
averaging runs at equal cost. E2 compares with the examiner, the second grader and the examiner's
second grading and runs the registered D2b test. Every error is given in grade points and as
students wrongly passed or failed. E3 compares `{python} EXP["E3"]["n_generators"]` generators and
`{python} EXP["E3"]["n_judges"][0]` judges, E4 the doctrinal fake answers and the quote check, and E5
the generated sheets for a second exam against its examiner's sheet.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

\draftnote{the answers per research question are written after E1 to E5}

*What the first iteration showed.* A generated grading sheet did not by itself make model grades
steadier. Across the five stronger judges, the sheet changed the run-to-run spread by almost nothing
on average, and one judge was steadier without it. The data cannot rule out a small effect either
way. The sheets also exposed a worse failure. With a detailed sheet, several judges gave nearly full
marks to answers that were empty or only repeated the facts of the case. GPT-5.6 Luna did so in
`{python} fc["tailored"][LUNA]["empty"]` of `{python} npas["tailored"][LUNA]["empty"]` runs on a
near-empty answer. An average agreement figure hides such failures. Every judge must therefore pass
tests with fake answers before use, and code must check that each point rests on words that stand in
the answer. Writing a sheet, grading with it and rating it are different skills. A model asked to
rate sheets preferred those that graded harshly, so sheet writer and judge should be chosen by how
close their grades come to human grades, not by how good a sheet looks.

```{python}
#| output: asis
if not all((_n, _x, _m, _gen_b)):
    print(r"\pending{what the expert exam shows, once the final D2 runs are in}")
else:
    _gm = [x for x in (_v(a, LU) for a in (G54, G54S, M1, M1S, M2, M2S)) if x]
    print(
        "*What the expert exam suggests so far.* On the examiner's own sheet, the best judge was about "
        f"{num(_x['mae'], 0)} of 100 points from the reference grades on average, or "
        f"{num(_x['mae_grade_points'], 0)} grade point{'' if num(_x['mae_grade_points'], 0) == '1' else 's'}, and ranked the scripts almost as the reference did. "
        f"Without a sheet the same judge was steady, but about {num(_n['bias'], 0)} points too generous, and it "
        "passed every student whom the reference fails. Generated sheets came close to the examiner's sheet "
        f"({num(min(x['mae'] for x in _gm), 0)} to {num(max(x['mae'] for x in _gm), 0)} points off), though "
        "mostly more generous. On this exam, then, a sheet did not make the judge steadier; it made its grades "
        "far more accurate. The platform's default judge was about "
        f"{num(_m['mae'], 0)} points off even on the examiner's sheet. A new sheet from the same generator "
        "moved a script's total more than a new run did, so a sheet should be fixed and approved once per "
        "exam. These are first readings on the scripts of one exam, and they favour the examiner's sheet "
        "(@sec-limitations).")
```

*Answers to the research questions.* \pending{one paragraph per research question after E1 to E5:
first a plain answer (yes, no, partly, not yet), then what it means in grade points and in students
wrongly passed or failed, then the number and its interval}

*What this means for exam practice.* Three points follow, all provisional. *Equal opportunity.* A
newly generated sheet can move a script's total by several points. A sheet should therefore be
generated once per exam, checked and approved by the examiner, and then used unchanged for every
candidate. *Accuracy.* The generated sheets tended to be generous. In practice feedback a student may
then believe they would pass when they would not. Such feedback should say so, or the sheet should
first be calibrated on a few scripts the examiner has graded. *Reasons.* Each point comes with a quote
that code has found in the answer, so an examiner or a student can see where it was earned. The code
confirms only that the words are there, not that they meet the requirement. The quotes can support
the examiner's reasons but cannot replace the examiner's own evaluation, which the examiner must make
personally [@bverwg2002_6C7_02]. The evidence so far supports feedback on practice exams with these
safeguards. A second reader that points the examiner to scripts where the totals differ is plausible
but untested. It does not support grading exams that count towards a degree without an examiner. EU
law classes AI that evaluates learning outcomes as high-risk (AI Act, Annex III, point 3(b)), with
the duties applying from December 2027 [@aiact2024; @omnibus2026]. Grading one script once costs
about `{python} num(100 * min(COST["judge_call_usd"].values()), 0)` to
`{python} num(100 * max(COST["judge_call_usd"].values()), 0)` US cents with the judges we priced
(Appendix \ref{sec-app-costs}). \pending{recommended pipeline and its cost per script}

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

*One expert exam.* D2 is one case in one area of law, graded on its author's sheet. D1 spans many
exams, but its human reference is noisy. Results on D2 may not transfer to other exams, areas or
examiners, and the second grader gives a human ceiling for one exam only.

*Each yardstick favours one grading basis.* The D2a reference grades were given on the examiner's own
sheet, and one setting grades with that same sheet. This favours it over generated sheets. On D1 all
human graders used the `{python} V["n_dims"]` general criteria that the judge without a sheet also
uses, which favours grading without a sheet. The second grader and the registered D2b test reduce
this bias but do not remove it.

*Open data questions.* For `{python} D2["d2a"]["grader_pending"]` D2a scripts the grader is not yet
confirmed, and the `{python} D2["d2a"]["later_case_text"]` scripts of 2024 are judged against a later
year's case text. The judge sees the current sheet also for scripts graded on an earlier version. The
D2b students saw model grades, made with an earlier quote check, before the author grades their
scripts; the author grades without seeing them.

*The exam author is a co-author.* The author wrote the exam, grades the scripts, reviews generated
sheets and co-writes this paper, and so knows the study's aims. Blind grading of D2b and the second
grader will limit this. The author reviews generated sheets without knowing their source (E3), but
this review is not independent.

*Development on the test exam.* During development, examples in the generator and judge prompts came
from the D2 exam. We replaced them with neutral examples, and code now checks every prompt for words
from the author's sheet. It matches words only and cannot rule out that the prompts were shaped while
the sheet was in hand. D2a is our development data, so results on it are optimistic.

*The quote check.* It confirms that a quote exists, not that it supports the credit (@sec-verifier).
It rejects some correct quotes and cannot catch a real sentence quoted for the wrong requirement.

*Models and settings.* GPT-5.6 Luna cannot be set to repeat its output. Even at its least random
setting, DeepSeek-V4-Pro's totals varied between runs (run-to-run spread
`{python} num(roster["deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro"]["repeat_sd"])` in the first iteration), so the
spread mixes the model, its settings and the provider's servers. Providers change and retire models;
we record model ids and dates.

*Exploratory design.* Only the test on D2b is registered in advance, and it runs once. Everything else
is exploratory. We report many comparisons without correcting for their number, and we added several
first-iteration settings after seeing earlier results.

*Scope.* All D2 scripts were typed. Handwritten exams would need transcription, which we did not
test. We did not test how examiners use a generated sheet or a model grade, for instance whether they
correct it or simply accept it.

# Ethics {#sec-ethics}

*Consent and personal data.* The students whose D2 scripts we use consented to research use, for the
`{python} D2["d2a"]["n_scripts"]` scripts of D2a and the `{python} D2["d2b"]["n_uploads"]` platform
submissions of D2b. The consent does not extend to sending their personal data to model providers.
All D2 texts are therefore pseudonymized and checked for personal data before any research call
(@sec-d2). The platform grades that the D2b students saw were produced in the normal use of the
platform, before this study. \pending{owner to confirm the wording on the platform-side grading and the providers' data terms}
D1 reuses the prior study's corpus under the consent obtained there, with pseudonymized graders
[@nagl2026bengerdata].

*Roles.* The exam author is a co-author, the source of the reference grades and the auditor of
generated sheets. We report this as a limitation and mitigate it with blind grading and a second
grader.

*Students who saw LLM grades.* The D2b students received LLM grades as feedback on a practice exam.
\pending{owner: whether and how students learn the expert grades}

*Use of the instrument.* Generated sheets are studied as a research instrument for evaluating and
supporting grading. They are not a replacement for human examiners in grade-bearing assessment, where
legal and pedagogical safeguards apply.

*Roth's sheet.* Gregor Roth agreed to be named and to have his sheet and workbook used. We report
only their structure, not their content.

# Data and code availability {#sec-availability}

The platform is open source under the Apache 2.0 license at
<https://github.com/SebastianNagl/benger-platform> \pending{tagged release or commit, archived with a
DOI}. It contains the judge, the quote check and the aggregation. The generator's instructions and
output specification, the validator, the allocation of points and the rendering of generated sheets
belong to a proprietary extension of the platform. \pending{owner decision: release of the generator
instructions, output specification and validator rules} The folder `publications/Transformation`
holds the analysis scripts and every aggregate this paper reports. Every run records the hashes of
its code, prompts and validator. Recomputing the aggregates needs data we do not release: the
per-call records of D1, which contain third-party exam text, and the private D2 and Z2 material.
D1's exam texts and the generated sheets, which restate the reference solutions, are not
redistributed. For D2 and Z2 we publish only aggregates (Appendix \ref{sec-app-datastatement}).

# AI usage {#sec-ai}

This section covers AI tools used to do the research and write the paper, not the models under
study. In the first iteration, the authors used OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol to discuss approaches and
Anthropic Claude Fable 5 to help write code and text. In the extended study, Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5
worked as a coding agent in the authors' repositories under the first author's direction. It wrote
the rebuilt pipeline (output specification and validator, checklist judge, quote check), the
experiment runner and all analysis scripts. It ran the experiments within budgets the first author
approved one by one. It drafted most of the text, tables and appendices, including this section. It
also searched the literature and checked the references it added against their sources. Further
instances of the same model, given identical instructions, reviewed the code, the data handling, the
statistics and the text in `{python} DZ["statistics"]["review_rounds"]` rounds, simulated one peer
review, and reviewed each section for readability and missing literature. The agent ran the scripts
that extracted and pseudonymized the D2 texts on the authors' machine, so parts of the raw scripts may
have reached Anthropic's service before pseudonymization. \pending{authors: confirm, and name the
terms under which this happened} \pending{authors: who wrote Section 2 and the legal parts of the
discussion} The authors checked \pending{every reference against its source; every number in the
abstract, discussion and tables; the quote check and the allocation code}. The authors set the
research questions and the design, supplied the exam, its grades and the sheets, decided every change
of scope and spending, and take full responsibility for the paper.

Table \ref{tab:glossary} glosses the German terms, Table \ref{tab:terms} the technical terms.

```{python}
#| output: asis
# Shared terms carry the companion paper's glosses word for word [@nagl2026bengerdata].
GLOSSARY_ROWS = [
    (r"\emph{Falllösung}", "Written case solution: the end-to-end work product that is graded."),
    (r"\emph{Sachverhalt}", "Fact pattern: the facts of the case the candidate works on."),
    (r"\emph{Gutachtenstil}", "Appraisal style: the conclusion follows the reasoning; the register graded here."),
    (r"\emph{Musterlösung}", "Expert reference solution against which submissions are graded."),
    (r"\emph{ausreichend}", "``Sufficient'': lowest passing grade (4-6 of 18 points)."),
    (r"\emph{Bewertungsbogen}", "Grading sheet: the expected solution split into steps, each worth a number of BE."),
    (r"\emph{Bewertungseinheiten} (BE)", "Assessment units: points on a grading sheet; 100 per exam here, in half points."),
    (r"\emph{Notenpunkte}", "Grade points: the statutory scale from 0 to 18 of German law examinations."),
    (r"\emph{Notenstufen}", "The seven named grades of that scale."),
    (r"\emph{Staatsexamen}", "State examination: the examination that gives access to the legal professions."),
    (r"\emph{Chancengleichheit}", "Equal opportunity: comparable candidates must be graded by comparable standards."),
    (r"\emph{Klausurschwerpunkte}", "The exam's focal problems."),
    (r"\emph{Maßstab}", "The standard a requirement is judged by: \emph{richtig} or \emph{folgerichtig}."),
    (r"\emph{richtig}", "Correct: judged against the correct law."),
    (r"\emph{folgerichtig}", "Consistent: judged against the candidate's own earlier decision."),
    (r"\emph{vertretbare Lösung}", "Defensible solution: one argued with sound reasons, which must not be marked as wrong."),
    (r"\emph{Folgefehler}", "Follow-on error: an error that later steps build on; it is not penalised twice."),
    (r"\emph{Weichenstellung}", "Structural fork: a defensible decision that changes the further structure of the solution."),
    (r"\emph{Lösungsweg}", "Alternative path after a structural fork, with its own steps."),
    (r"\emph{Vertretbarkeitsanforderungen}", "The reasoning that makes an alternative path defensible."),
    (r"\emph{Hilfsgutachten}", "Auxiliary opinion: the part a candidate still owes after a decision that ends the case."),
    (r"\emph{Arbeitsergebnis}", "Work result, such as an opinion or a draft judgment."),
    (r"\emph{Kardinalfehler}", "Cardinal error: an error grave enough to limit the grade as a whole."),
]
write_table("tbl_glossary", "German terms used in this paper and their glosses.", "tab:glossary",
            ["Term", "Gloss"], GLOSSARY_ROWS, colspec="lp{0.66\\textwidth}", size=r"\footnotesize")
TERMS_ROWS = [
    ("Judge", "A language model that grades an answer."),
    ("Generator", "A language model that writes a grading sheet from the case and its reference solution."),
    ("Code", "A fixed program, not a model: it computes points, checks rules and quotes, and adds up totals."),
    ("Run", "One grading of one answer. The same judge can grade the same answer several times."),
    ("Run-to-run spread", "How far a judge's total for the same answer moves between runs (standard deviation)."),
    ("Average error (MAE)", "The mean distance between a model's total and the human grade, in points."),
    ("Bias", "The mean signed distance: positive if the model is too generous, negative if too strict."),
    ("$r$", "Whether two graders rank the answers in the same order (1: the same order); a constant shift does not count."),
    (r"$\kappa$", "Agreement on pass or fail, corrected for the agreement expected by chance."),
    ("95\\% interval", "The range in which the true value lies with 95\\% confidence, from redrawing the exams or scripts many times."),
    ("Dependability", "The share of the spread of totals that reflects real differences between scripts (0 to 1)."),
    ("Fake answers (probes)", "Made-up answers, such as an empty one or a copy of the case, that must score about zero."),
    ("Quote check", "Code that tests whether each quote of the judge stands in the answer."),
    ("Validator", "Code that checks a generated sheet against fixed rules and sends errors back to the generator."),
    ("Scoring unit", "What the judge scores: each requirement (met, partly met, not met) or each step (points)."),
]
write_table("tbl_terms", "Technical terms used in this paper.", "tab:terms", ["Term", "Meaning"], TERMS_ROWS,
            colspec="lp{0.66\\textwidth}", size=r"\footnotesize")
```

# First-iteration details {#sec-app-first}

This appendix gives the details of the first iteration that Section \ref{sec-first} summarizes, and
Tables \ref{tab:compliance} to \ref{tab:probes} give its results per generator, judge and fake answer.

*Generation (RQ3).* `{python} V["n_valid"]` of `{python} V["n_cells"]` generator–exam cells hold a
valid sheet. `{python} V["n_full"]` generators covered every exam; Llama-4 Maverick covered
`{python} gen_s[llama]["valid"]` and GPT-5.4 Mini `{python} gen_s[MINI]["valid"]`, mostly because
feedback did not repair broken references of alternative paths. Of `{python} G["series_total"]`
dispatched series, `{python} G["series_failed"]` failed: `{python} G["failed_by_stage"]["provider"]`
aborted at the provider (all GPT-5.4 Mini, credit errors), `{python} G["failed_by_stage"]["contract"]`
failed validation and `{python} G["failed_by_stage"]["parse"]` failed parsing. First-attempt
compliance over all series that reached the model spans
`{python} pct(G["first_attempt_range_model_series"][0])` to
`{python} pct(G["first_attempt_range_model_series"][1])`. Counted over valid sheets only, GPT-5.4 Mini
looks better than it is: `{python} pct(gen_s[MINI]["first_attempt_rate_valid"])` there, but
`{python} pct(gen_s[MINI]["first_attempt_rate_model_series"])` over the series that reached the model
(`{python} gen_s[MINI]["first_attempt_successes"]` of `{python} gen_s[MINI]["model_series"]`) and
`{python} pct(gen_s[MINI]["first_attempt_rate_all_series"])` over all `{python} gen_s[MINI]["series"]`
of its series (Table \ref{tab:compliance}). Generators did not converge: mean step counts range from
`{python} num(G["step_count_mean_range"][0], 1)` to `{python} num(G["step_count_mean_range"][1], 1)`,
and stated weight sums from `{python} num(G["weight_sums"]["min"], 0)` to
`{python} num(G["weight_sums"]["max"], 0)`. A lexical screen found vague formulas that the prompt
itself bans in `{python} G["lexical_screen"]["listed"]` of `{python} G["lexical_screen"]["n_rubrics"]`
sheets (`{python} G["lexical_screen"]["any"]` with near variants). The generation prompt asked for
"exactly `{python} CONTRACT["bounds"]["total_points"]` raw points" in its first line, while its
weighting rule said that no exact sum was needed because code normalizes; we disclose this as an
ambiguity. The weight class was shown to the judge but played no part in the arithmetic.

*Variance (RQ1).* For Luna, the run-to-run SD falls from `{python} num(REL["holistic_luna"]["repeat_sd"])`
(no sheet) to `{python} num(REL["tailored_luna"]["repeat_sd"])` (zero-shot sheet) and
`{python} num(REL["fewshot_luna"]["repeat_sd"])` (sheet written from an example, few-shot). The direction is consistent, but no single step is established:
few-shot minus no sheet is `{python} sgn(lf["point"])` (`{python} ci(lf["ci95"])`; sign test
$p$ = `{python} pv(lf["sign_p"])`), zero-shot minus no sheet `{python} sgn(lz["point"])`
(`{python} ci(lz["ci95"])`; $p$ = `{python} pv(lz["sign_p"])`), and few-shot minus zero-shot
`{python} sgn(lfz["point"])` (`{python} ci(lfz["ci95"])`; $p$ = `{python} num(lfz["sign_p"])`). Across
the `{python} V["n_matched"]` judges other than GPT-5.4 Mini that graded both ways, the zero-shot effect averages
`{python} sgn(pooled["point"])` (`{python} ci(pooled["ci95"])`; Table \ref{tab:contrasts}). This is the
unweighted mean of the per-judge differences, without correction for multiple comparisons. Only
Sonnet's per-judge interval excludes zero, and it points the adverse way: Claude Sonnet 4.6 is steadier
without a sheet (`{python} sgn(son_f["delta"])`, `{python} ci(son_f["ci95"])`). For the
weakest judge, GPT-5.4 Mini, the run-to-run SD rises from
`{python} num(REL["holistic_mini"]["repeat_sd"])` to `{python} num(REL["tailored_mini"]["repeat_sd"])`
(`{python} sgn(mini_f["delta"])`, `{python} ci(mini_f["ci95"])`, clustered by exam; cell-level sign
test $p$ = `{python} pv(mz["sign_p"])`, Wilcoxon $p$ = `{python} pv(mz["wilcoxon_p"])`). The steadiest
few-shot sheets, a post-hoc subset by generator, reached `{python} num(min(fs_sd.values()))` with
Luna, and an in-sample floor (the best sheet per exam, chosen after the fact)
`{python} num(CO["trend_luna"]["in_sample_floor"])`; both are optimistic bounds without intervals.
These contrasts use step sums; on the stored totals they differ by at most
`{python} num(CONTRAST_SHIFT)`.

*Agreement (RQ2).* Against the mean human grade, Luna's $r$ moved from
`{python} cor(AG["luna"]["hol"]["r"])` to `{python} cor(AG["luna"]["zs_step_sum"]["r"])` and
`{python} cor(AG["luna"]["fs_stored"]["r"])`, and its bias flipped from

a sheet ($r$ = `{python} cor(AG["mini"]["hol"]["r"])`, MAE
`{python} num(AG["mini"]["hol"]["mae"], 1)`) but not with the sheet: $r$ =
`{python} cor(AG["mini"]["zs_step_sum"]["r"])`, MAE `{python} num(AG["mini"]["zs_step_sum"]["mae"], 1)`,
an increase of `{python} sgn(AG["mini"]["mae_zs_minus_hol"]["point"], 1)`
(`{python} ci(AG["mini"]["mae_zs_minus_hol"]["ci95"], 1)`). Few-shot sheets left it there ($r$ =

Leave-one-exam-out bias correction shows that the error of the prior study's control judge was
mostly a level shift (MAE `{python} num(C["legacy_control"]["mae"], 1)` to

not (`{python} num(AG["luna"]["zs_step_sum"]["mae"], 1)` to
`{python} num(AG["loeo_calibrated_mae"]["tailored_luna"], 1)`).

*Judges and probes.* The `{python} len(JU["roster"])` roster judges graded all answers against the drawn sheets
(Table \ref{tab:judges}). Apart from Mini they reached $r$ `{python} cor(JU["capable_r_range"][0])`
to `{python} cor(JU["capable_r_range"][1])`; Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Terra, one run each,
`{python} cor(extra["claude-opus-5"]["r"])` and `{python} cor(extra["gpt-5.6-terra"]["r"])`. A set of

`{python} fc["fewshot"][LUNA]["empty"]` of `{python} npas["fewshot"][LUNA]["empty"]` few-shot runs, with
`{python} num(PR["luna_empty_mean_failing"]["tailored"], 1)` and
`{python} num(PR["luna_empty_mean_failing"]["fewshot"], 1)` points on average when it did (median
`{python} num(FL["luna_empty_median_failing"]["value"]["tailored"], 1)` and
`{python} num(FL["luna_empty_median_failing"]["value"]["fewshot"], 1)`), but in `{python} fc["holistic"][LUNA]["empty"]` runs without a sheet.
GPT-5.4 Mini failed `{python} PR["mini_negative_fails"]["tailored"]` of
`{python} PR["mini_negative_passes"]["tailored"]` runs on negative fake answers with the sheet and
`{python} PR["mini_negative_fails"]["holistic"]` without a sheet, but its failures without a sheet
 were small (median `{python} num(sev["holistic"][MINI]["empty"]["median"], 0)` points on the
empty answer) and its sheet failures near-total (median
`{python} num(sev["tailored"][MINI]["empty"]["median"], 0)`). Under the sheet, the off-topic answer scored at most
`{python} num(max(v for j, v in PR["offtopic_max_tailored"].items() if j != MINI), 1)` points with every
judge except Mini (up to `{python} num(PR["offtopic_max_tailored"][MINI], 0)`). All
`{python} sum(1 for v in PR["positive_control"]["tailored"].values() if v == "pass")` judges passed the
positive control under the sheet; Mini failed it without a sheet in
`{python} PR["positive_control_fails"]["holistic"][MINI][0]` of
`{python} PR["positive_control_fails"]["holistic"][MINI][1]` runs. On one answer that only restates
the case, Mini under the sheet gave `{python} ", ".join(num(v, 0) for v in AG["p01"]["mini_zs"].values())`
points and Luna `{python} ", ".join(num(v, 0) for v in AG["p01"]["luna_zs"].values())`.

The first-iteration pipeline had no quote check and a generic system prompt. Its response schema listed the steps in storage order (by key length, then bytes),
not in outline order, and the steps of alternative paths had no response keys, so a judge had to
move credit for another path onto the replaced steps, where the per-step cap dropped any overflow
\pending{number of alternative paths affected}. Budget neutrality thus held in the document, not in
scoring. The new pipeline changes all of this at once, so E0 and E3 test the weaker judges again
before we claim anything about them.

*Generators and the audit (RQ3).* A crossed sweep graded each exam's answers under every valid sheet
of that exam: `{python} GE["n_rubrics"]` sheets and `{python} GE["n_rubric_pick_cells"]` sheet–answer
cells, Luna, `{python} passes` runs (Table \ref{tab:generators}). An automated audit by GPT-5.4 Mini
rated each blinded sheet on `{python} GE["audit"]["n_dimensions"]` dimensions from 1 to
`{python} GE["audit"]["scale_max"]`. Within exams, the audit total shows no linear association with
grading error ($r$ = `{python} cor(link["mae_centered"]["pearson"])`,
`{python} cic(link["mae_centered"]["ci95"])`; Spearman `{python} cor(link["mae_centered"]["spearman"])`)
and a weak one with stability ($r$ = `{python} cor(link["repeat_sd_centered"]["pearson"])`,
`{python} cic(link["repeat_sd_centered"]["ci95"])`; Spearman
`{python} cor(link["repeat_sd_centered"]["spearman"])`). It correlates with the *absolute* bias
($r$ = `{python} cor(link["abs_bias_centered"]["pearson"])`, `{python} cic(link["abs_bias_centered"]["ci95"])`)
and with the signed bias ($r$ = `{python} cor(FL["audit_signed_bias_link"]["value"]["pearson"])`,
`{python} cic(FL["audit_signed_bias_link"]["value"]["ci95"])`): higher-rated sheets grade harsher. At the generator level
($n$ = `{python} GE["generator_level_spearman_audit_vs_bias"]["n"]`), higher audit totals go with
harsher grading (Spearman `{python} cor(GE["generator_level_spearman_audit_vs_bias"]["luna"])` with
Luna, `{python} cor(GE["generator_level_spearman_audit_vs_bias"]["sonnet"])` with Sonnet): the Claude
sheets top the audit (`{python} num(gpo[opus]["audit_total"], 1)` and
`{python} num(gpo[sonnet]["audit_total"], 1)` of `{python} GE["audit"]["n_dimensions"] * GE["audit"]["scale_max"]`)
and grade among the harshest (bias `{python} sgn(gpo[opus]["bias"], 1)` and `{python} sgn(gpo[sonnet]["bias"], 1)`).
DeepSeek-V4-Flash sheets cut agreement ($r$ = `{python} cor(gpo[dsf]["validity_r"])`, the lowest)
behind a mid-field audit (`{python} num(gpo[dsf]["audit_total"], 1)`). Llama-4 Maverick sheets made
Luna least stable (repeat SD `{python} num(gpo[llama]["repeat_sd_mean"])`), but the audit ranked them
lowest (`{python} num(gpo[llama]["audit_total"], 1)`), so this failure was visible. GPT-5.4 Mini, the
weakest judge and least compliant generator, ranked among the best sources on the exams where it
produced a sheet (paired $\Delta$MAE `{python} sgn(gpo[MINI]["paired_dmae"], 1)` on `{python} gpo[MINI]["n_rubrics"]` exams), but
its probability of ranking first is `{python} cor(mini_rank["p_top1"])` and the estimate is conditional
on survival. The ranking replicates moderately with Claude Sonnet 4.6 as judge (one run; Spearman
`{python} cor(GE["lens_spearman"])`; `{python} cor(GE["lens_spearman_full_coverage"])` among
full-coverage generators). Few-shot generation raised Mini's valid sheets from
`{python} G["zeroshot_compliance_mini"]["valid"]` to `{python} G["fewshot_compliance"][MINI]["valid"]` of
`{python} G["fewshot_compliance"][MINI]["total"]`; since the few-shot setting also used its own pool of
`{python} V["n_fs_gens"]` generators, its effects are confounded with that pool.

*Weights and step size.* The generated weights carry a small, judge-dependent signal
(Appendix \ref{sec-app-weights}). Re-aggregating the stored per-step scores, Luna keeps most of its agreement with
class weights alone ($r$ `{python} cor(ws_j[LUNA]["class_only"]["r"], 3)` vs
`{python} cor(ws_j[LUNA]["actual"]["r"], 3)`) and loses some with uniform weights
(`{python} cor(ws_j[LUNA]["uniform"]["r"], 3)`). For DeepSeek-V4-Pro, class weights do worse than uniform
ones (`{python} cor(ws_j["deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro"]["class_only"]["r"], 3)` vs
`{python} cor(ws_j["deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro"]["uniform"]["r"], 3)`). Uniform weights lowered the run-to-run
SD for `{python} len(ws_s["uniform_lowers_repeat_sd"])` of `{python} ws_s["n_judges"]` judges, and the
actual weights beat `{python} num(100 * ws_s["perm_share_range"][0], 0)` to
`{python} pct(ws_s["perm_share_range"][1])` of within-sheet permutations. The judges saw the actual step
maxima, so these re-aggregations are conditional on them. Big steps are not noisier per point
(Appendix \ref{sec-app-steps}). Steps of `{python} SS["summary"]["bucket"]` points held
`{python} pct(ss[LUNA]["share_points"])` of the points and, for most judges, a larger share of the
summed per-step variance (Luna `{python} pct(ss[LUNA]["share_variance"])`). But if every step had the
same relative noise they would hold `{python} pct(ss[LUNA]["share_squared_maxima"])`, because variance
grows with the square of a step's points; only
`{python} ", ".join(SHORT.get(j, NAME[j]) for j in SS["summary"]["above_equal_relative_noise"]) or "no judge"`
exceeded that, and Luna's relative SD on big steps (`{python} num(ss[LUNA]["rel_sd_big"], 3)`) was no
higher than on steps of 3 to 5 points (`{python} num(ss[LUNA]["rel_sd_3_5"], 3)`). The case for small
steps is averaging: independent errors on many small steps partly cancel, while the error on one big
step enters the total whole. Step count correlated only weakly with error
($r$ = `{python} cor(GE["granularity"]["steps_vs_mae_r"])`) and with repeat SD
(`{python} cor(GE["granularity"]["steps_vs_repeat_sd_r"])`). The new generator writes small steps.

# Apportionment audit {#sec-app-apportionment}

The audit re-derives the points of all `{python} AP["n_rubrics"]` first-iteration sheets
(`{python} AP["n_steps"]` steps) from their stated weights under each routine of Table
\ref{tab:apportionment}. A step lies outside its fair range when its points differ from its quota by
a full unit or more; an order inversion is a pair in which the lighter step receives more points.
The as-run routine is reproduced exactly by a copy of the original code.

# Weight sensitivity {#sec-app-weights}

Every first-iteration judgment stores a score and a maximum per step. Re-weighting the stored
fractions shows how much the generated allocation contributes to agreement and stability without new
judge calls (Table \ref{tab:weights}). *Actual* reproduces the step sums; *class* weights each step by its
weight class (routine `{python} num(WS["summary"]["class_weights"]["routine"], 0)`, load-bearing
`{python} num(WS["summary"]["class_weights"]["tragend"], 0)`, focal `{python} num(WS["summary"]["class_weights"]["schwerpunkt"], 0)`); *uniform* counts every step the same; *permuted* shuffles a sheet's own
points across its steps. The judges saw the actual maxima, so every scheme is conditional on them.

```{python}

                  pct(w["permuted"]["share_of_permutations_below_actual_r"]),
                  num(w["actual"]["repeat_sd"]), num(w["uniform"]["repeat_sd"])])
write_table(
    "tbl_weights",
    "Weight sensitivity of the first-iteration sheets: agreement $r$ with the human pool under five weight "
    "schemes, the share of within-sheet permutations whose $r$ falls below the actual one, and repeat SD under "
```

# Step size and variance {#sec-app-steps}

For every judge with at least `{python} passes` runs per answer, we sum the per-step variance across runs by
step size and compare it with the share of points in that size class (Table \ref{tab:steps}). The
share ignores covariance between steps, so it is a share of *summed* step variance. The right
comparison is the share of *squared* points: if every step had the same relative noise (SD
proportional to its points), a size class would hold exactly that share of the variance. The
relative SD (SD over points) of big steps and of steps of 3 to 5 points tests this directly.

```{python}
#| output: asis
srows = []
for j in sorted(ss, key=lambda j: -ss[j]["ratio"]):
    v = ss[j]
    srows.append([NAME[j], v["n_cells"], v["n_step_cells"], pct(v["share_points"], 1),
                  pct(v["share_squared_maxima"], 1), pct(v["share_variance"], 1),
                  num(v["rel_sd_big"], 3), num(v["rel_sd_3_5"], 3)])
write_table(
    "tbl_steps",
    f"Steps of {SS['summary']['bucket']} points in the first-iteration sheets: answers and step cells, share "
    "of points, share of squared points (the variance share under equal relative noise), share of summed "
    "per-step repeat variance, and the relative SD of these steps and of steps of 3 to 5 points.",
    "tab:steps", ["Judge", "Answers", "Step cells", "Points", "Points$^2$", "Variance", "Rel. SD", "Rel. SD 3--5"],
    srows, size=r"\footnotesize")
```

# Precision {#sec-app-precision}

This appendix shows how large a difference must be before the data can reveal it. The paper uses
$\alpha$ = .05 throughout; the column for $\alpha$ = .025 is kept for comparison. The minimum
detectable effect of a paired contrast is
$(t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1} + t_{\text{power},\,n-1})\,\sigma_d/\sqrt{n}$. We take $\sigma_d$ from the
closest existing contrast, Luna with and without a generated sheet on D1, so the values are
planning proxies (Table \ref{tab:mde}). The D2 proxy uses the D1 human reference, which is noisier
than step-by-step expert grades; the first D2a runs show smaller spreads, and @sec-prelim reports the
detectable differences they imply.

```{python}
#| output: asis
c1, c2 = MDE["C1_repeat_sd"], MDE["C2_abs_error_vs_expert"]
NLBL = {"n_15_d2a": f"D2a ({D2['d2a']['n_scripts']} scripts)",
        "n_38_all_distinct": f"all distinct D2 scripts ({D2['distinct_scripts']})",
        "n_37_dependent_pair_once": f"D2, dependent pair once ({D2['n_counting_dependent_pair_once']})"}
mrows = [["Repeat SD, D1", c1["n"], num(c1["sd_of_differences"]), num(c1["mde"]["alpha_0.025"]), num(c1["mde"]["alpha_0.05"])],
         [f"Repeat SD, D1, {int(next(k for k in c1 if k.startswith('mde_') and 'passes' in k).split('_')[1])} runs (optimistic)", c1["n"], "",
          num(c1["mde_5_passes_optimistic"]["alpha_0.025"]), num(c1["mde_5_passes_optimistic"]["alpha_0.05"])]]
for k, lbl in NLBL.items():
    m = c2["mde"][k]
    mrows.append([f"Absolute error, {lbl}", "", num(c2["sd_of_differences"], 1), num(m["alpha_0.025"], 1),
                  num(m["alpha_0.05"], 1)])
write_table(
    "tbl_mde",
    f"Minimum detectable effects at power {cor(DZ['statistics']['mde_power'], 1)} ($t$-based, paired). "
    "$\\sigma_d$: SD of the paired differences in the proxy contrast.",
    "tab:mde", ["Contrast", "$n$", "$\\sigma_d$", "$\\alpha$ = .025", "$\\alpha$ = .05"], mrows,
    colspec="lrrrr", size=r"\footnotesize")
```
